lessons.title: Create your first SwiftUI iOS app
lessons.summary: Make a small greeting app. Learn what Xcode builds, where it runs, and how the app describes its first screen.
objectives: Create a practice iOS app and find the code that starts it.
Explain the product to build, the build plan, the SDK, the oldest supported iOS, and the place to run.
Follow App to Scene to View to see how the first screen is described.
Record compiler outcomes and simulator launch observations as separate checks.

sections.title: Start with one greeting
sections.html:
Start with one screen that says hello. Xcode is the Mac app used to write, build, and run this iOS app. A project groups files and settings. A target describes one product to build. A scheme chooses an action, such as Build or Run, and its settings. A destination says where that action runs, including a simulator's device and iOS version. You already distinguish Android source, build tasks, and devices. Keep those choices separate here too; the Xcode names do not each mean a Gradle variant.

The greeting uses synthetic data, meaning made-up values for practice. You need a Mac with Xcode, its iOS SDK, and an installed simulator runtime. Create a practice iOS App target with iOS 17 as its deployment minimum for this track. Xcode 15 or later provides the Swift 5.9-era features used in later examples. Those are the course's starting requirements; they do not claim to name today's newest toolchain. A newer compiler can be used. Lesson 070 supplies the Swift language practice, so no earlier iOS project is required.

A successful compiler result, a running simulator app, and a working preview are separate observations. Record each when you actually perform it. This course supplies source and acceptance expectations; it has not executed your new app. Keep the company checkout as reading material and create the scratch project outside its app targets.

sections.title: Choose what Xcode will build
sections.html:
An app template is a starting set of files and settings. Open Xcode and choose File → New → Project, then the iOS App template. Name the product FirstSteps. Choose SwiftUI for the interface and Swift for the language. The wording can vary between Xcode versions. Leave database setup off for now. Include a unit-test target if offered; you can add it later. The organization identifier, such as example.learning, helps form the bundle identifier. That identifier names the app product. The module name used in Swift imports is a separate setting.

Save to a learner-owned directory. In the project navigator, select the project and then the app target. Find its minimum deployment setting and set iOS 17. The deployment target means the oldest supported runtime; the installed SDK means which API declarations the compiler can see. Selecting an iOS 17 simulator does not independently change that target setting. Swift language mode is another setting; it controls language rules and diagnostics rather than deciding the simulated operating system.

Inspect the generated app entry source and the initial ContentView source. Source membership matters: a visible file must belong to the app target or its synchronized source folder. Keep generated resource catalogs. Replace the generated entry declaration and initial view with the complete example below, using one source file if convenient. Remove the old declarations from that scratch target so there is exactly one @main type and no duplicate root type. The example needs no downloaded package, account data, image asset or custom font.

sections.title: Follow the code from start to screen
sections.html:
The entry point is the code that starts an executable. Here @main marks that entry. This complete example belongs in an iOS 17+ app target. import SwiftUI makes SwiftUI's types available. FirstStepsApp: App says the type follows the App protocol's requirements. Its computed body returns a scene description. some Scene leaves the concrete type unnamed for callers while the compiler knows it. A scene is a system-managed place to present content. WindowGroup supplies content for that family of windows. It does not promise several visible windows on every device.

import SwiftUI

@main
struct FirstStepsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup {
            WelcomeView()
        }
    }
}

struct WelcomeView: View {
    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            Image(systemName: "hand.wave")
                .font(.largeTitle)
            Text("Hello, Demo Ada")
                .font(.title)
            Text("My first iOS screen")
                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

The trailing closure is the block written after a call's parentheses. Inside WindowGroup's block, WelcomeView() makes a root view description. It follows View, and its computed body supplies more description through some View. VStack places the children vertically. spacing: names the gap input, measured in points. Text describes the made-up visible words. Each dot call adds a modifier to the previous description. The final padding adds space around the stack. Reading this code describes the screen; it starts no request and writes no file.

The braces after WindowGroup and VStack contain builder expressions rather than an imperative list of addView calls. SwiftUI creates and updates platform rendering from those descriptions. The hand.wave string names a system symbol; it is distinct from a named asset in your bundle. Lesson 072 explains those resources and controls, and lesson 073 examines the modifier chain more closely.

sections.title: Build, launch, and read the greeting
sections.html:
A simulator runs an app in a simulated Apple device environment on your Mac. Choose the app scheme, then an installed iPhone simulator whose iOS meets your deployment minimum. If it is missing, check Xcode's runtime settings and Devices and Simulators window. The device definition needs its matching runtime, the software that runs that iOS version. Product → Build compiles the app. Product → Run installs and launches it. A generic iOS device can be useful for building, but it is not a specific simulator that can show this greeting.

This simulator exercise does not require provisioning a physical phone or enrolling in a distribution program. If you encounter a signing complaint, first check whether you accidentally selected a physical or generic device rather than the simulator. Real-device execution and distribution have separate setup and entitlement boundaries; they are not needed to prove this greeting. Avoid changing company signing settings to make the learner target run.

Look for both text lines and the symbol. Stop the app from Xcode, change Demo Ada to Demo Lin, and run again. This confirms that the source belongs to the selected product and that you are observing the new build. A stale simulator app or a second similarly named scheme can otherwise mislead you. Write down scheme, configuration, deployment minimum, destination and observed output; these details make a later failure reproducible.

sections.title: Find which step failed
sections.html:
A compiler turns Swift source into a program and reports source errors. If it cannot find SwiftUI, first check the target and SDK. This example needs an Apple-platform target. If it reports a second entry point or duplicate type, look for generated declarations you left in that target. If a file never builds, check target membership: whether this product includes that file. If an API is unavailable, compare its required iOS version with your deployment minimum. A newer SDK can know an API that an older supported runtime cannot use.

If Build succeeds but Run fails, read the Run report and destination status. An unavailable runtime, failed installation and application crash are different problems. If the screen is blank, verify WindowGroup's root and any conditional branches. Use Xcode's issue navigator for compiler messages and the report navigator for action logs. Do not begin by deleting broad directories or reinstalling every tool. A small greeting has few dependencies, so the first actual error usually identifies the relevant boundary.

The active booking demo has an App entry that constructs ContentView inside WindowGroup. Its Tuist manifest separately declares app, unit-test and UI-test products and an iOS 18.2 deployment minimum. That checkout setting is verified source evidence, not our scratch minimum or a universal requirement. It also has company module dependencies and font registration. Your standalone example intentionally uses system resources so it can teach app setup without reproducing that environment.

sections.title: Explain your first app to another engineer
sections.html:
A handoff is a short record that lets another engineer repeat your work. Explain this path: the scheme builds the app target; the single entry describes a WindowGroup; WelcomeView describes a VStack; SwiftUI renders the children. A VStack places those children vertically. Also explain which files are actually compiled into the target. A file appearing in Xcode's navigator does not by itself prove membership. Android projects also separate files, build tasks, and runtime devices. An Xcode scheme does not replace every Gradle product-flavor choice.

Add a third Text for a synthetic build note, then predict where it appears and why. Change the title font separately from the stack spacing. Small isolated changes build confidence that you understand the code instead of only recognizing a template. Keep a notebook of actual Build and Run results, including errors you resolved. A preview can be added in lesson 074; it will speed iteration while leaving launch and lifecycle checks necessary.

The course companion lives at labs/SwiftUIWorkbench. Read its README and actual project settings before using it. Your greeting remains a complete exercise on its own. Compare the companion's entry and target settings with your own only after checking the files. The existence of that companion does not establish that your greeting built or ran.

lessons.title: Views, controls, assets, and SF Symbols
lessons.summary: Build a form with ordinary controls. See how edits reach stored values and how bundled images differ from Apple's system symbols.
objectives: Read the labels in control calls and find where each control writes its edits.
Tell an image in the app bundle from an SF Symbol supplied by iOS.
Choose controls with the right action and accessibility behavior, and explain why keyboard choices do not validate input.
Write a button action that changes only the intended values.

sections.title: Give each control one clear job
sections.html:
A control is an interface element that knows how a user can interact with it. Text displays words. TextField edits a String. Toggle edits a true-or-false value. Button runs an action. Picker chooses one value from a set. Start with the type that fits the user's job. A Button already supplies activation and accessibility behavior. An image with a tap gesture would need more work to provide those behaviors. Android offers the same broad choice between a standard control and a custom gesture, with different framework rules.

This lesson's complete source belongs to one scratch iOS 17+ app target using Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated App and ContentView declarations with this source, retaining only one entry point. It uses system resources and synthetic input. A Form organizes controls in platform-styled rows; lesson 077 studies editing and collection management in more detail. The controls here are intentionally ordinary so you can recognize the framework vocabulary before studying a company design system.

The @State declarations make the controls interactive. For now, read them as locally owned in-memory values managed by SwiftUI; lesson 075 develops the lifetime contract. A leading dollar sign projects read/write access for a control. It is not Kotlin string interpolation. Passing a normal String to the text argument of TextField would not express where the user's edits should go.

sections.title: Read what each control receives
sections.html:
An argument label names an input at a Swift call site. In TextField("Display name", text: $name), the first input has no written label. It supplies the field's description. text: names the binding input, the read and write access used for edits. The first string is not the current field value. $name points edits to name. Likewise, Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $reminder) needs a binding to a Boolean. Reading those labels shows both what a control displays and which source it changes.

A trailing closure is a block passed after the call's parentheses. Button uses one for its action. That block runs when the button is activated; describing the screen does not run it. The action can assign state. The final Text uses a ternary expression, the condition ? first : second form, to choose what to display. It reads name rather than keeping a second summary String in sync. This demo uses an empty String to mean no name. An optional value, which can be absent, is a different choice taught later.

Stepper's 1...5 range includes one and five, so count cannot step beyond those limits. Picker uses Int tags because priority is an Int. A tag is the value that represents an option; a tag of the wrong type can fail to match the selection. Slider edits a Double between zero and one. Text uses a percentage formatter to display it. DatePicker edits a Date, Apple's value for an instant in time, while showing calendar-date components. Display depends on calendar and time zone. This control fixture does not define a full scheduling rule.

import SwiftUI

@main
struct ControlsApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { ControlsScreen() } }
}

struct ControlsScreen: View {
    @State private var name = ""
    @State private var reminder = false
    @State private var count = 1
    @State private var priority = 0
    @State private var progress = 0.5
    @State private var date = Date()

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Section("Synthetic note") {
                Label("Learning card", systemImage: "book")
                TextField("Display name", text: $name)
                    .textInputAutocapitalization(.words)
                Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $reminder)
                Stepper("Copies: \(count)", value: $count, in: 1...5)
                Picker("Priority", selection: $priority) {
                    Text("Normal").tag(0)
                    Text("High").tag(1)
                }
                Slider(value: $progress, in: 0...1)
                Text(progress, format: .percent.precision(.fractionLength(0)))
                DatePicker("Practice date", selection: $date,
                           displayedComponents: .date)
            }
            Section("Resources and actions") {
                Image(systemName: "star.fill")
                    .foregroundStyle(.orange)
                    .accessibilityHidden(true)
                Button("Fill demo values") {
                    name = "Demo Ada"
                    reminder = true
                }
                .buttonStyle(.borderedProminent)
                Text(name.isEmpty ? "No name" : name)
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.title: Choose a system symbol or a bundled image
sections.html:
A bundled asset is a named resource included with your product. Image("DemoBadge") looks for that resource in the relevant bundle. An SF Symbol is a symbol image supplied by iOS. Image(systemName: "star.fill") asks for one by name. The initializer tells you which lookup occurs. Android resources provide a useful comparison, but Apple's bundle and symbol rules are their own. Check symbol availability for your supported iOS versions. A symbol shown in the installed SF Symbols app may need a newer OS than your app supports.

To practice a bundled image, open the scratch app's asset catalog, create an image set named DemoBadge and add your own synthetic illustration. Ensure the catalog is included in the app target. Then replace the decorative symbol with Image("DemoBadge").resizable().scaledToFit().frame(maxHeight: 80). Resizable permits image scaling; scaledToFit preserves its aspect ratio within the proposed space. Without resizable, a frame does not necessarily resize the underlying bitmap. Do not paste that variation before creating the named asset.

Asset catalogs also support colors and appearance variants. A named color uses Color("DemoAccent") after creating that color resource. Verify light and dark variants rather than hard-coding a dark foreground on a dark background. For a package or framework resource, the appropriate bundle may need to be passed explicitly; a directory name is not itself a runtime bundle identifier. Keep the baseline code independent of custom assets so a missing resource cannot obscure the syntax exercise.

sections.title: Make labels and input help clear
sections.html:
A Label combines readable text with an icon. Label("Learning card", systemImage: "book") gives both parts one meaning. Accessibility features help people perceive and operate the interface in different ways. This example hides the decorative star from accessibility because nearby text already gives the information. An icon that performs an action should be a Button with a useful label. An image that conveys unique information needs an accessible description. Decide from its job; hiding every image would lose meaning.

Keyboard settings help with entry. They do not check a product rule. Word capitalization can suit a display name but alter an identifier incorrectly. A number-pad keyboard does not prevent someone pasting letters. A disabled Button shows that an action is currently unavailable; an important rule should also be checked inside that action. Lesson 077 checks trimmed input when Add runs. That keeps the user's typing intact while still rejecting an empty name at the point it matters.

System fonts and controls respond to environment and accessibility settings. Prefer font roles such as title and body over assuming all labels fit a fixed pixel box. A button style changes appearance while keeping Button semantics. Here borderedProminent gives the fill action visual emphasis; it does not make that action a save operation. The reminder Boolean is merely synthetic UI state, with no notification request or permission side effect.

sections.title: Trace a control that seems broken
sections.html:
A constant binding is access to a fixed value; writes do not change it. It can show a frozen preview, but it cannot demonstrate editing. If typing has no effect here, check the binding's source and the file's target membership before adding a callback. If Fill changes the name while another field stays unchanged, inspect the variable passed to that field. Two similarly named variables are still two separate sources. For a Picker, check that selection and tags use the same type and that the selected option exists.

If an image is blank, identify whether the initializer names a bundle asset or a system symbol. For an asset, check exact capitalization, catalog membership and bundle selection. For a symbol, check spelling and OS availability. For distorted artwork, review resizable and the aspect-ratio modifier before adding a second frame. A failed resource lookup and a view with unsuitable size are different boundaries.

The active address form uses framework controls through company wrappers, including its text-field wrapper and explicit keyboard and content-type settings. Those names require company modules and cannot be imported into this tiny scratch app. Read that anchor to recognize how a public control boundary can be decorated with design and analytics policy. Do not infer that every custom wrapper validates all input or that the source was executed during this course audit.

sections.title: Predict exactly what Fill and Reset change
sections.html:
State means the values the screen currently uses. Activate Fill demo values and predict its state changes first: name and reminder change because the action assigns them. The field, Toggle, and summary display those same sources. Count, priority, progress, and date keep their values because the action leaves them alone. This distinction matters even when every control looks fine afterward. Before adding Reset, write down exactly which fields it should change. Then implement that rule, rather than clearing everything because it is convenient.

Use the simulator to check keyboard entry, the Stepper bounds and both Picker choices. Try a long synthetic display name and a larger text setting; note any clipping rather than declaring the screen universally adaptive. A preview can later provide these fixtures quickly, but actual keyboard and focus behavior requires suitable interactive checks. Save the source and your observed sequence as the evidence for this lesson.

For an interview, explain one initializer from the type of its binding through the resulting UI behavior. A strong answer names the value owner, the activation boundary and the resource lookup. Listing control names alone cannot explain why a form updates. These first distinctions are the building blocks for reusable views and explicit data flow in the next lessons.

exercise.solution:
Add Button("Reset inputs") { name = ""; reminder = false; count = 1 } inside the actions Section. This matches the written rule: clear the name, turn the reminder off, and return count to one. Priority, progress, and the chosen date keep their values. If the product should clear those too, first change its stated rule. lessons.title: Compose views with stacks and ordered modifiers
lessons.summary: Arrange views in rows, columns, and layers. Read modifier calls in order so you can predict spacing, background size, and state lifetime.
objectives: Arrange children with HStack, VStack, and ZStack and explain their row, column, and layer relationships.
Explain how generic content and a view builder produce typed screen descriptions.
Predict how padding before or after a background changes the colored area.
Find the layout cause of overflowing content instead of changing identity at random.

sections.title: Put children beside, below, or over each other
sections.html:
A stack is a container that arranges child views. HStack puts them in a row. VStack puts them in a column. ZStack puts them in overlapping layers. Compose's Row, Column, and Box offer a familiar starting idea. Their exact measuring rules differ. In SwiftUI, a parent proposes sizes and children respond with sizes. A stack does not simply assign a UIKit frame to every descendant. Learn these ordinary relationships first. Session 031 later teaches custom layout when your content needs more than a row or column.

This complete example belongs to a scratch iOS 17+ app target, using Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated entry and root declarations, keeping one App entry. It includes a generic card and all its types; no company helpers or earlier source files are required. The code uses ScrollView so a taller set of examples can remain reachable. A scroll view is not automatically a good substitute for every List or Form; the container's interaction and data needs still guide that choice.

Extract a subview when it has a useful name and responsibility. Here InfoCard owns the common title, padding and background, while the caller supplies its contents. The card does not own the user's draft or load data. A reusable visual boundary and a long-lived state owner are different design decisions, even if both appear as types named View.

sections.title: Read the card's type and content block
sections.html:
A generic type takes another type as an input. Content: View means InfoCard's Content type must follow the View protocol. The card stores one value of that chosen type. () -> Content describes a closure with no inputs that returns content. @ViewBuilder lets the caller write supported groups of view expressions and conditional branches in that closure. This initializer calls the closure while making the card value, then stores its result. It does not keep the closure as a later button action.

An opaque return type lets the compiler know a concrete type without requiring callers to name it. That is what some View does in the computed body property. The body's view-builder support combines supported expressions into that type. Containers can therefore accept several child expressions without an explicit array. You do not write return before each child. Builder syntax has rules; it is not any arbitrary loop that adds platform view objects. For data-driven repetition, use ForEach, introduced in lesson 077.

import SwiftUI

@main
struct CompositionApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { CompositionScreen() } }
}

struct InfoCard<Content: View>: View {
    let title: String
    private let content: Content

    init(title: String, @ViewBuilder content: () -> Content) {
        self.title = title
        self.content = content()
    }

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            Text(title).font(.headline)
            content
        }
        .padding(16)
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
        .background(.yellow.opacity(0.15),
                    in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}

struct CompositionScreen: View {
    var body: some View {
        ScrollView {
            VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 20) {
                InfoCard(title: "Synthetic reading plan") {
                    HStack(alignment: .top, spacing: 12) {
                        Image(systemName: "book")
                        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 4) {
                            Text("Demo chapter")
                            Text("A longer subtitle can wrap onto another line.")
                                .foregroundStyle(.secondary)
                        }
                        Spacer(minLength: 0)
                    }
                }
                ZStack(alignment: .topTrailing) {
                    RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12)
                        .fill(.blue.opacity(0.15))
                        .frame(height: 100)
                    Text("New").padding(8)
                }
                Text("Padding then background")
                    .padding(12).background(.orange.opacity(0.3))
                Text("Background then padding")
                    .background(.orange.opacity(0.3)).padding(12)
            }
            .padding()
        }
    }
}

The title: label identifies the title input, while the trailing closure provides content. self.title names the card's stored property so it is distinct from the initializer parameter. Swift infers the Content type from the supplied HStack. AnyView is a type-erasing wrapper: it hides a view's concrete type behind one common view type. You do not need that wrapper just because a generic type looks complex. Keep the compiler's known Content type here. Choose type erasure later only when a real interface boundary needs it.

sections.title: Use gaps, alignment, and flexible space
sections.html:
Alignment says where children line up. The outer VStack aligns at leading and uses twenty-point gaps. Leading follows reading direction, so it can change sides with the language. The inner HStack aligns at the top, placing the symbol beside the top of the text group. Its inner VStack uses four-point gaps so title and subtitle read as one group. Points are layout units rather than physical pixels. Choose gaps for the content relationship. Do not use them to hide a guess about a particular device's width.

Spacer asks for flexible empty space. The zero minimum permits it to shrink when the row is narrow. It is useful for pushing content apart, but multiple spacers and fixed widths can compete and make a row unreadable. A frame with maxWidth: .infinity asks the wrapper to expand to the finite space offered by its parent, not to render an infinitely wide window. Its leading alignment positions the child within that wrapper.

ZStack draws later children over earlier children. In this example the background rectangle supplies a one-hundred-point demonstration area, and New is placed at its top trailing corner. This fixed height is a fixture for a simple badge area, not a universal layout policy for text-heavy cards. An overlay can decorate an existing view without using an independent ZStack as the main layout container; choose it when the decoration should follow the base view's size rather than establish a separate area.

sections.title: Predict the result of each modifier
sections.html:
A modifier returns a new view description around the previous result. With padding then background, the color covers the padded area. With background then padding, the color covers the original text area and the later margin stays uncolored. Predict both before running the example. Nothing randomly changes order: each background belongs to the description it receives. Compose also makes modifier order matter, but you must still learn SwiftUI's exact layout and drawing rules.

A frame is a sizing and alignment wrapper. It does not force dimensions onto every descendant. Clip cuts drawing that extends outside a shape; it does not repair a bad text-width choice. Offset moves where a view is drawn without reserving that extra space for neighbors. Padding does reserve layout space. That is why offset can cause overlap while padding can separate items. Start with the child, then draw each wrapper in order to find which operation caused the result.

Font and foregroundStyle can flow through the view environment to applicable descendants, while individual child modifiers can override inherited choices. Applying a headline to a whole container can affect more text than expected. The InfoCard explicitly sets its header font and leaves its content's choices available to the caller. RoundedRectangle is a shape description used by background; its corner radius changes decoration, not the model's identity or the existence of a touch action.

sections.title: Describe the screen without starting work
sections.html:
Body is a computed description of the screen. SwiftUI may evaluate it repeatedly during updates. Keep requests, file writes, and state changes out of that calculation. A subtitle can read current input. A request started while constructing a VStack can run again without a clear owner. Put user work in actions and ongoing work in a defined task scope. Moving the request into another computed view property does not fix its lifetime; that property can still run while SwiftUI asks for the screen description.

Conditional branches can change structural identity. If a child owns local state and you replace it with a different branch, the old storage may disappear. Wrapping a view in a new random id to fix layout makes state preservation worse. Choose stable structure where the same feature continues, and deliberate identity replacement where a new feature instance should begin. Lesson 075 gives a concrete editing experiment.

The repository's address demo uses VStack and HStack for its debug panel and action row. Read its padding then background chain at the verified anchor and explain the same wrapper relationship. The advanced flow layout in session 031 handles a different problem: variable-width wrapping with an explicit measurement policy. You do not need that machinery to build this first card, and its source is not evidence that your card was rendered or measured.

sections.title: Check long text before adding more frames
sections.html:
Dynamic Type is the user's text-size setting. Try a long subtitle, a narrow window, and a large text size. If the row leaves too little readable width, a column may fit the content better. If the background is narrow, check whether the expanded frame comes before it. If New covers useful text, decide whether that badge should take its own layout space. Each fix should identify a container or wrapper and explain the result. Shrinking text or adding frames at random hides the cause rather than establishing a usable layout.

Separate layout observation from correctness in other domains. A visually pleasing card does not establish keyboard access, VoiceOver labels or persistence. Use text-specific and window-specific fixtures now, then conduct the broader adaptive checks in lesson 082. Record actual observations, including any truncation, and keep the example synthetic. A novice should leave this lesson able to draw the approximate wrapper tree and justify every stack, instead of memorizing an incantation of padding and frame calls.

lessons.title: Previews and safe fixture injection
lessons.summary: Use made-up sample data to preview a view. Give editable previews real state, and record preview, build, and launch results separately.
objectives: Create named previews for fixed sample data and for a view you can edit.
Explain which features need compiler support and which need a particular iOS version.
Supply each preview's data and services where that preview is created.
Say what preview rendering proves and which launch and interaction checks remain.

sections.title: Try the view with known sample data
sections.html:
A preview lets you inspect one view without opening the whole app flow. Like a Compose preview, Xcode's preview uses a development host. A host is the environment that builds and runs the selected content. It can execute initializers, body calculations, and tasks. This matters when choosing services: a preview that constructs a real service can cause real work. Start with known made-up inputs, not a production account. The goal is a small case that another engineer can reproduce and understand.

Begin with explicit synthetic inputs. A fixture is known sample data chosen to expose a behavior: an ordinary name, an empty name, a long name, a loading state or a failure state. Fixtures are not copied user records. A preview describes which fixture and environment to use. Keeping those choices in a named scenario makes a visual issue reproducible and lets another engineer understand which case a screenshot represents.

The complete example targets a scratch iOS 17+ app with Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated App and root types, retaining one executable entry. It uses no company modules, network services or disk store. The same FixtureHost can be launched as the real app root, so preview and app behavior share the editing description while remaining different execution checks.

sections.title: Check the compiler and iOS requirements separately
sections.html:
A macro asks the compiler to expand marked source into supporting code. #Preview is a macro introduced with Xcode 15's Swift toolchain. The hash marks macro use; it is not a normal runtime call. Named closures provide the content. The compiler must support the macro, the preview tools must run it, and the view's APIs must support the chosen iOS. For example, the SwiftUI Observation integration used later needs iOS 17 regardless of which preview spelling you choose.

Do not infer that every SwiftUI #Preview needs an iOS 17 deployment minimum. Apple's Xcode 15 release notes describe previewing SwiftUI content for older OS versions with an appropriate availability annotation. UIKit and AppKit preview forms also have their own requirements. This track chooses iOS 17 to keep the first examples simple. For an older product, read the actual compiler diagnostic and release notes before raising its deployment minimum just to fix a preview. The macro's tooling requirement and the content's runtime requirement are separate checks.

The older PreviewProvider pattern remains a useful alternative for toolchains or targets where the chosen macro configuration is unsuitable. Its static previews property returns content. The small alternative below is complete for its view and can be placed in an appropriate SwiftUI app target; it is not a second app entry. It does not make an unavailable API inside that view become available.

import SwiftUI

struct LegacyGreeting: View {
    var body: some View { Text("Synthetic preview").padding() }
}

struct LegacyGreeting_Previews: PreviewProvider {
    static var previews: some View { LegacyGreeting() }
}

This lesson deliberately uses a stateful wrapper rather than declaring local wrapper state with newer preview-only conveniences. You can explore APIs such as Previewable separately with their actual toolchain requirements; they are unnecessary for a reliable iOS 17 fixture.

sections.title: Pass the sample values directly
sections.html:
Injection means supplying inputs where you create a view or service. FixtureCard accepts name and status as ordinary values. It does not need to guess whether the process is a preview. Its synthesized initializer, the initializer Swift creates from stored properties, accepts those values. CardFixture groups known made-up strings. Its static properties belong to the type rather than individual instances. That grouping is convenient sample data; it is not a global service owner. A named preview can now select an input openly, making both the test case and its intended result clear.

import SwiftUI

enum CardFixture {
    static let ordinary = "Demo Ada"
    static let long = "Demo Ada with a deliberately long synthetic display name"
}

struct FixtureCard: View {
    let name: String
    let status: String

    var body: some View {
        VStack(alignment: .leading, spacing: 12) {
            Text(name.isEmpty ? "No display name" : name).font(.title2)
            Text(status).foregroundStyle(.secondary)
        }
        .padding()
        .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)
        .background(.blue.opacity(0.1),
                    in: RoundedRectangle(cornerRadius: 12))
    }
}

struct FixtureHost: View {
    @State private var name = CardFixture.ordinary

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            TextField("Demo name", text: $name)
                .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
            FixtureCard(name: name, status: "Fixture only: no request")
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

@main
struct FixturesApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { FixtureHost() } }
}

#Preview("Editable fixture") {
    FixtureHost()
}

#Preview("Long name, large text") {
    FixtureCard(name: CardFixture.long, status: "Offline fixture")
        .padding()
        .environment(\.dynamicTypeSize, .accessibility2)
}

#Preview("Empty, dark") {
    FixtureCard(name: "", status: "No record selected")
        .padding()
        .preferredColorScheme(.dark)
}

Each preview constructs the complete view it needs. The long-name scenario injects an accessibility Dynamic Type size through the environment. The dark scenario requests a dark appearance. These modifiers make the selected variants explicit. They do not cover every device width, locale or assistive technology. Use Xcode's canvas device controls to inspect further size variants, and label any exported observation with the actual setup.

A preview of FixtureCard does not automatically inherit dependencies installed on the app's WindowGroup, because it instantiates that card directly. Later, if a component reads a required environment model or ModelContext, its preview must install that dependency too. Supply a synthetic model or in-memory container at the preview boundary rather than patching the view to silently use a production singleton when missing.

sections.title: Give edits somewhere real to go
sections.html:
An interactive fixture needs a writable source. FixtureHost owns name in State, SwiftUI's storage tied to the host's identity. The field gets a binding to that source. The card gets the current String for display. Typing changes the source that both use, so the card can update. A temporary local variable inside a preview closure does not establish the same SwiftUI storage relationship. Use a small host view whose ownership you can explain. The host can also be the app root, giving you a separate place to check the same editing flow.

A constant binding is acceptable when deliberately inspecting a frozen control. Writes into it do not update the constant, so it cannot demonstrate a successful editing interaction. For editable child components, create a small host like FixtureHost, or pass a real observable fixture owned at an appropriate boundary. State ownership is still independent of persistence; stopping or recreating the preview can discard this name.

A deterministic service fixture gives a known result for the chosen input. Supply one when a preview needs a service. A success case and an error case should work without a real account or public internet. Keep loading out of body. If a preview uses a task, that task should call the supplied fixture. A class named MockLoader could still call a real service inside its implementation. Read what it does before relying on the name. That keeps both the chosen behavior and the work it starts under your control.

sections.title: Find why the preview failed
sections.html:
A diagnostic is a message explaining a compiler or runtime problem. If the canvas fails, begin with the target's compiler diagnostics. Missing imports, a second app entry, unavailable APIs, and missing resources can prevent the host from building. Check the scheme, destination, runtime, and whether the source belongs to the target. A framework view may need its resource bundle as well as its Swift code. Identify the failed dependency before clearing caches or adding delays. Those actions cannot tell you whether the original problem was code, resources, or preview setup.

If the preview displays an empty state unexpectedly, trace the actual input value. If typing does nothing, confirm you are using an interactive/live preview mode and a changing binding. If repeated refreshes start requests, inspect initializers and lifecycle tasks for real service construction. A preview can rerun those paths; its development context is not a lifecycle guard. First reproduce the same view in the scratch app root to distinguish canvas infrastructure from component behavior.

The active booking address view provides normal, error and prefilled previews, constructs explicit models and registers its company fonts. That source shows why resource and dependency setup matter. Your scratch example uses system fonts and plain inputs, so copying the font registration would add an unnecessary company dependency. The verified source anchors support the comparison; reading them does not prove those previews rendered successfully here.

sections.title: Record what each preview actually shows
sections.html:
Evidence is what you observed in a specific check. Try the ordinary, empty, and long-name cases. Compare light and dark appearance, narrow space, and larger text. For each result, record the scenario name, device or destination, text size, and visible issue. A screenshot captures that one rendering. It leaves launch, navigation, accessibility focus, restart, and cancellation as separate checks. Keep lesson 071's simulator Run check even when previews work. A good record lets another engineer repeat a visual case without mistaking it for a complete app test.

Keep fixture construction near the boundary and production component logic reusable. If a missing dependency crashes a preview, add the dependency to the fixture host rather than weakening the component's contract silently. The long-name case should remain synthetic and intentionally awkward; visual coverage improves when fixtures challenge assumptions. Lesson 082 turns these experiments into a broader adaptive and accessibility checklist, while this lesson establishes the small repeatable inputs that make that later work practical.

lessons.title: Local state, bindings, and view identity
lessons.summary: Give a draft one owner and let child controls edit it through bindings. Check when edits stay, when fields clear, and when a new editor starts.
objectives: Choose one place to own an editable local draft.
Pass read and write access to a child instead of making another copy.
Tell a redraw, a change of stored values, and a replacement of view identity apart.
Write rules for switching records and for what, if anything, survives restart.

sections.title: Choose one place for the draft
sections.html:
The source of truth is the value everyone reads and edits. In Compose, moving state to a parent makes that owner clear. SwiftUI's Binding packages access to an owner's value. Ask who creates the draft and who decides to discard it. If a parent owns one String and a child makes a private copy, you now have two sources to coordinate. A live summary can instead read the same source as the field. That gives both views current data without callbacks that keep duplicate summary text in sync.

This lesson uses a scratch iOS 17+ app target with Xcode 15 or later, although State and Binding themselves support older SwiftUI systems. Replace the generated app/root declarations with the complete example, keeping one executable entry. The LocalDraft struct contains ordinary stored values. The editor owns one instance in State and exposes only the access its controls need. Nothing saves to disk or sends data externally.

State is storage that SwiftUI manages for a view identity, its matched place in the interface. Recreating the View struct gives a new description; it does not automatically replace that stored draft. Keep owned State private so callers do not treat it as ordinary input they can continually overwrite. The declaration looks like a value property, but SwiftUI decides which storage belongs to the current identity. This distinction explains how a small value-based view can keep edits through routine updates.

sections.title: Use a binding to edit the parent's value
sections.html:
A property wrapper adds behavior around a property declaration. @State private var draft = LocalDraft() asks SwiftUI to manage this source. Private limits direct access from outside the type. @Binding var name: String gives the child access to a source held elsewhere; it does not create another name store. The dollar sign in $draft.name supplies a binding to the nested String. This lets the child field edit the parent's value. It is read and write access, rather than a snapshot copied into the child.

import SwiftUI

struct LocalDraft {
    var name = ""
    var reminder = false
}

struct NameEditor: View {
    @Binding var name: String
    var body: some View {
        TextField("Demo display name", text: $name)
            .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder)
    }
}

struct LocalEditor: View {
    @State private var draft = LocalDraft()
    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            NameEditor(name: $draft.name)
            Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $draft.reminder)
            Text(draft.name.isEmpty ? "No name" : draft.name)
            Button("Clear fields") { draft = LocalDraft() }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

struct StateHost: View {
    @State private var renderCount = 0
    @State private var identity = 0

    var body: some View {
        VStack(spacing: 16) {
            Text("Parent events: \(renderCount)")
            LocalEditor().id(identity)
            Button("Unrelated parent event") { renderCount += 1 }
            Button("Replace editor identity") { identity += 1 }
        }
        .padding()
    }
}

@main
struct StateLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { StateHost() } }
}

The synthesized NameEditor initializer accepts the binding as name:. Inside the child, name reads the current wrapped String and $name forwards its binding to TextField. Those forms refer to different capabilities: value access versus a read/write handle. A plain let name: String would be enough for a display-only child, but not for this field.

The clear action assigns a fresh LocalDraft value to the existing state location. Because this is a struct, changing its fields follows value semantics rather than creating a shared reference graph. The summary reads the current name directly. Repeated rendering does not require a listener to copy the field into another summary variable. The struct's memberwise/default initialization and property basics were practiced in the language track; here the new element is SwiftUI's storage relationship.

sections.title: Redraw the description or replace the editor
sections.html:
View identity is how SwiftUI matches an interface position between updates. Type Demo Ada, then activate Unrelated parent event. The counter changes, so SwiftUI can ask for new descriptions. The editor keeps the same structural place and explicit identity, so its draft stays. LocalDraft() supplies the starting value for new storage. It is not an instruction to erase existing storage whenever body is evaluated. Predict both the new counter and the unchanged draft before running this experiment. Counting body calls alone cannot tell you whether state was replaced.

Now activate Replace editor identity. The host increments identity, so .id(identity) describes a different editor identity. SwiftUI can discard the old editor-associated state and create new storage initialized from LocalDraft. This is an intentional teaching experiment. A random UUID created on every body evaluation would repeatedly change identity and could erase edits during routine updates. Stable IDs are correctness inputs, not just animation hints.

The hierarchy itself also contributes identity. Switching between distinct conditional branches or removing a view can end its local state lifetime. State does not promise survival across arbitrary removal, process termination or scene reconstruction. Navigation and container behavior can preserve some views in a flow, but you should choose the actual owner for any draft that must outlive a particular editor. Moving the source to a common parent is often clearer than hoping a transient child stays alive.

sections.title: Decide what a new record should do
sections.html:
A seed is the initial input used to create new storage. An editor may copy a record's name into State in its initializer. If that editor keeps its identity, a later parent input does not continually replace the local State. That can protect unsaved typing. It can also leave an old draft visible if the parent switches records without a replacement rule. Decide which behavior the product needs. Initialization starts a draft; it does not, by itself, define how every future server or parent update should change that draft.

Choose a clear rule. A parent can own the draft and provide bindings. A child can receive a new identity when its record changes. A model can expose an explicit replace-record action. For unsaved typing, decide whether a server refresh may overwrite it or whether confirmation or merging is needed. Two onChange callbacks that copy data both ways do not define which value wins. They can hide loops and lost edits. State the precedence rule before writing synchronization code.

A custom Binding can receive get and set closures, functions that read and write its source. They can transform values at an interface boundary. Use that power deliberately. Trimming or uppercasing on every keystroke can move the cursor or interfere with text input methods. Often it is clearer to derive eligibility while typing and normalize only when the user accepts the input. A binding gives access. It does not by itself validate the value, make several changes one atomic transaction, save to disk, or make shared access thread-safe.

sections.title: Decide how long the draft must last
sections.html:
Lifetime means how long a value or owner remains available. Here a parent event keeps the draft because editor identity stays the same. Clear fields changes values in that storage. Replace identity ends that editor's state lifetime and creates a new one. Process restart creates a new in-memory app because this example has no saved draft. Avoid calling all four events reset without explaining which one you mean. A product rule should say whether it clears values, starts another editor, or restores a previously saved draft.

State is not an Android ViewModel store, SavedStateHandle or database. The analogy to remember helps explain identity-associated storage, but it does not import Android lifecycle or restoration guarantees. AppStorage and SceneStorage serve selected storage needs with distinct limitations, while SwiftData later supplies a real record store. Do not choose persistence because an annotation's name sounds like state ownership.

The active address demo uses State for its model reference and a separately retained coordinator. Its model uses Observation, which lesson 076 will explain. The verified source demonstrates local ownership but does not prove disk restoration. A weak delegate also needs a retaining owner regardless of whether UI reads are observed. Keep the language's value/reference distinction, SwiftUI's storage distinction and disk lifetime distinction separate.

sections.title: Find why edits disappeared or diverged
sections.html:
A disconnected draft means the field and summary no longer use the same source. If edits disappear, check changing IDs, conditional branches, and owner placement. If the field changes while the summary stays old, trace both inputs. A constant-binding preview intentionally keeps a fixed source. A child that copies its binding into another State value can also diverge. Begin with the source and its lifetime before blaming redraws. Repeated screen-description work is allowed; the goal is to make ownership correct through those updates.

Use the complete host to create a repeatable sequence: type Demo Ada, toggle Reminder, trigger the parent event, clear fields, type again, then replace identity. Predict each result before running it. A notebook of values and identity events is more useful than logging every body evaluation and assuming more evaluations indicate a leak. SwiftUI is allowed to evaluate descriptions frequently; your ownership contract should remain correct.

The next lesson moves from a local value draft to a shared observable reference model. It does not replace the principle of one source. It introduces a separate observation mechanism and explicit reference lifetime, with a legacy alternative for older code. Carry the source-of-truth diagram into that change instead of selecting wrappers from their names alone.

lessons.title: Observation and model ownership, including legacy code
lessons.summary: Let an editor and summary share one model. Learn which wrappers own it, expose edits, or observe changes in modern and older SwiftUI code.
objectives: Explain UI change tracking, instance ownership, safe access rules, and disk saving as separate jobs.
Use State for the modern model owner, Bindable for edits, and ordinary references for display.
Use StateObject and ObservedObject with models that actually follow ObservableObject.
Check that name validity and Reset use the one shared model.

sections.title: Share one model between editor and summary
sections.html:
A reference lets several consumers use the same object instance. Here an editor and summary share a ReadingDraft. The owner chooses where that object lives and when it is replaced. Its class declaration alone does not notify SwiftUI when a field changes; it also needs change tracking. An Android state holder shared between components is a useful starting idea. SwiftUI's ownership and Observation rules still differ from Android ViewModel and StateFlow. Trace creation, storage, and property reads in this example instead of assuming one familiar annotation supplies all those jobs.

This complete modern example belongs to a scratch iOS 17+ app target using Xcode 15 or later. Swift's Observation macro was introduced in the Swift 5.9 era, and SwiftUI's integration used here requires iOS 17. Replace the generated app and root declarations with the supplied source, keeping one entry point. Foundation provides whitespace trimming, Observation supplies the macro, and SwiftUI supplies the owner storage, binding adapter and controls.

The lesson is an executable-sized introduction to ideas mentioned in old session 009. It walks from the model declaration to consumers rather than assuming the reader already knows where an iOS model comes from. The synthetic ReadingDraft is in memory; adding a class and observation does not save a record, schedule notifications or retain every delegate connected to it.

sections.title: Separate change tracking from safe access
sections.html:
A macro generates supporting code at compilation. @Observable adds Observation support for the type's eligible properties. It does not allocate view-associated State storage. final class makes a reference type that cannot be subclassed. Name and reminder are mutable fields. canContinue is a computed Boolean: it trims the current name and checks whether anything remains. Deriving that answer avoids maintaining a second validity flag after every edit. The stored name itself keeps what the user typed; the validity calculation does not rewrite the field.

Isolation means rules about where code may access shared state. @MainActor adds those rules separately from Observation. Calls and mutations must obey the main actor's contract. This example also marks the owner and consumers MainActor. Observation alone does not make background writes safe. Actors serialize access to isolated state; they are not one dedicated thread per model. The main actor is associated with main-thread UI work. Keep long CPU calculations off that UI path and return safe results through a suitable worker boundary.

import Foundation
import Observation
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
@Observable
final class ReadingDraft {
    var name = ""
    var reminder = false

    var canContinue: Bool {
        !name.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty
    }

    func reset() {
        name = ""
        reminder = false
    }
}

@MainActor
struct ObservedEditor: View {
    @Bindable var draft: ReadingDraft

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Demo name", text: $draft.name)
            Toggle("Reminder", isOn: $draft.reminder)
            DraftSummary(draft: draft)
            Button("Reset") { draft.reset() }
        }
    }
}

@MainActor
struct DraftSummary: View {
    let draft: ReadingDraft
    var body: some View {
        Text(draft.canContinue ? draft.name : "Enter a name")
    }
}

@MainActor
struct ObservedRoot: View {
    @State private var draft = ReadingDraft()
    var body: some View { ObservedEditor(draft: draft) }
}

@main
@MainActor
struct ObservationLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { ObservedRoot() } }
}

The reset method changes two properties on the same object. Every consumer holding that reference sees the updated values under the observation contract. The reference's identity has not changed. A let reference in DraftSummary prevents reassignment of that property, but it does not make the referenced object's fields immutable. Use API/access-control design when a capability really must be read-only; let alone is not a security boundary.

sections.title: Keep the owner, editor, and reader distinct
sections.html:
State keeps ObservedRoot's locally created model reference for that root identity. Passing draft to ObservedEditor passes the same instance. Bindable gives the editor projections such as $draft.name, so controls can edit its fields. It does not create another draft or save one to disk. DraftSummary can receive a plain reference because it only needs to read for display. These declarations express different jobs: holding the chosen instance, exposing edit access, and reading current data. None removes the need to choose when the model should be discarded.

A dependency here is a property read that helps produce the screen. SwiftUI tracks observable reads made while evaluating body. The summary reads canContinue, and that getter reads name. When it can continue, it also reads name for display. Relevant changes can therefore update the description. Keep these getters simple enough to trace. You do not need to subscribe every view to every field with one broad global notification just to display a name.

Do not recreate ReadingDraft inside the editor's body and pass that fresh object to every child. That would lose the intended stable source. Avoid side effects in model initialization, because candidate construction can happen during description creation even when SwiftUI retains existing state storage. If the model is supplied by an app-level or feature-level owner, pass that reference in; the receiving view need not pretend to create ownership by copying it into private local state.

sections.title: Match older wrappers to the older model
sections.html:
Older SwiftUI code often uses Combine change tracking. ObservableObject is its model protocol. Published announces changes to its wrapped properties. A creating view uses StateObject to keep a stable instance of that model. A receiving view uses ObservedObject to subscribe to a supplied instance. Both can retain references while in use. ObservedObject does not provide the same stable creator-owned instance if the caller keeps constructing new models. First read the actual model declaration, then choose the wrapper that fits it. Similar names are not enough to make the modern and older systems interchangeable.

The following declarations are a complete alternative root and model for that pattern. They can be used in a scratch SwiftUI app supporting iOS 14+; StateObject arrived in iOS 14. Set the app's WindowGroup to LegacyRoot instead of ObservedRoot if practicing this alternative, and do not add a second app entry. It uses no Observation-only model.

import Combine
import SwiftUI

@MainActor
final class LegacyDraft: ObservableObject {
    @Published var name = ""
}

@MainActor
struct LegacyEditor: View {
    @ObservedObject var draft: LegacyDraft
    var body: some View { TextField("Demo name", text: $draft.name).padding() }
}

@MainActor
struct LegacyRoot: View {
    @StateObject private var draft = LegacyDraft()
    var body: some View { LegacyEditor(draft: draft) }
}

ReadingDraft uses Observation; it does not follow ObservableObject, so StateObject cannot simply wrap it as the older example does. A legacy ObservableObject also does not become a modern observable model just by changing its owner to State. Read the actual type's protocol conformance, property annotations, subscribers, and owner. A migration may need to preserve Combine publishers, tests, delegates, and older-iOS support. Publishers deliver values to subscribers under their own contract. Replacing annotation names without tracing these relationships can lose behavior even when the new owner declaration looks familiar.

sections.title: Ask who retains it and who saves it
sections.html:
Retention means holding a strong reference so an object remains alive. Ask separately how the UI hears changes, who retains the chosen instance, and what survives restart. Here Observable supplies change tracking and root State keeps the local reference. There is no persistent store. A destination can share that draft while the root owner remains. A new process creates a new default model. The object being observable does not establish retention for weak delegates or storage on disk. Follow each of those relationships when reading company models.

An environment can distribute a model to descendants but does not by itself define a business lifetime. A feature-owned model might be cleared on leaving a flow, while an app-owned model might survive several screens. Account changes and unsaved drafts need product decisions. Sharing a class everywhere can increase accidental lifetime and coupling, so do not create a singleton merely to keep typing from disappearing.

The active address demo locally owns its observable form model and separately retains a coordinator because the model's delegate is weak. The active member-ID demo receives a legacy model with ObservedObject. These source anchors demonstrate coexistence. They do not prove a migration is complete, establish the supplying member-ID owner's lifetime, or imply the form persists data. Follow those boundaries when studying the advanced sessions rather than generalizing from one annotation.

sections.title: Check shared edits and computed validity
sections.html:
Eligibility is the rule for whether the user may continue. Type spaces into name, then Demo Ada. The computed rule rejects spaces and accepts the meaningful name. It trims only to check; it leaves typed input in the name source. Toggle the reminder, then Reset. Reset clears both fields on the existing object, without replacing its reference. An unrelated root event should also preserve that reference under stable identity. These checks let you distinguish changes to fields from creating another model or losing its owner.

If the summary remains stale, check whether it received the same object and whether body reads the observable property. If typing resets, inspect owner placement and identity. If a mutation triggers an actor-isolation diagnostic, fix the call boundary instead of removing MainActor without reasoning. If callbacks disappear, inspect weak receiver retention rather than assuming Observable keeps delegates alive.

Record model behavior separately from visual rendering. A unit test can prove canContinue and reset under MainActor without proving focus or layout. Lesson 084 will supply a tested capstone pattern. For now, a strong ownership explanation names model creation, binding access, read dependencies and the absent disk contract; that is more useful than calling every model a ViewModel.

lessons.title: Lists, forms, editing, search, and refresh
lessons.summary: Add and edit notes with stable IDs. Delete the right note after search, and refresh without throwing away local edits.
objectives: Give each editable row an ID that stays the same when its title or position changes.
Keep typing separate from the Add action's validation.
Turn filtered delete positions into source IDs, and state when reordering is allowed.
Await refresh directly and explain how it handles cancellation and local edits.

sections.title: Choose a collection and give each row an ID
sections.html:
A List describes a scrolling collection with platform row behavior. A Form groups input controls. A ScrollView scrolls its content, but it does not supply all the same editing behavior. Choose the container from what the user needs to do. Android RecyclerView and Compose LazyColumn already teach you to separate data from visible rows. Carry that idea here while learning SwiftUI's own rules. An identity contract means deciding what continues to name a row when its title, position, or visible state changes. That choice supports editing and deletion correctly.

The complete source targets a scratch iOS 17+ app with Xcode 15 or later. Replace the generated App and root declarations, keeping one entry. All types are included, and all notes are synthetic. NavigationStack gives rows a place to push their editor, but typed path design is deferred to lesson 079. The store is a local State array, so no records survive process restart.

ReadingNote conforms to Identifiable by providing an immutable UUID. That UUID is created when the note is constructed, not each time body reads it. Title is mutable display data, so it is unsuitable as the identity of an editable note. Two notes may also legitimately have the same title. Stable identity keeps editing, deletion and later selection associated with the record rather than its current position or label.

sections.title: Read repeated rows and their edit access
sections.html:
ForEach describes repeated child content from data. [ReadingNote] is an array of notes. ForEach(visibleNotes) makes a row description for each identifiable note in the visible subset. The closure receives that note value. In filter, $0 names the first closure input without writing a parameter name. Filtering selects matches without changing notes. localizedCaseInsensitiveContains compares user-facing text while ignoring case under localized rules. It does not define database identity or turn display titles into permanent record keys.

import Foundation
import SwiftUI

struct ReadingNote: Identifiable {
    let id: UUID
    var title: String
    var finished = false
    init(id: UUID = UUID(), title: String) {
        self.id = id
        self.title = title
    }
}

struct NoteEditor: View {
    @Binding var note: ReadingNote
    var body: some View {
        Form {
            TextField("Title", text: $note.title)
            Toggle("Finished", isOn: $note.finished)
        }
        .navigationTitle("Edit note")
    }
}

@MainActor
struct NotesScreen: View {
    @State private var notes = [
        ReadingNote(title: "Demo arrays"),
        ReadingNote(title: "Demo bindings")
    ]
    @State private var query = ""
    @State private var newTitle = ""
    @State private var refreshMessage = "Not refreshed"
    @State private var refreshToken: UUID?

    private var visibleNotes: [ReadingNote] {
        notes.filter { query.isEmpty || $0.title.localizedCaseInsensitiveContains(query) }
    }

    private func binding(for snapshot: ReadingNote) -> Binding<ReadingNote> {
        Binding(
            get: { notes.first(where: { $0.id == snapshot.id }) ?? snapshot },
            set: { updated in
                guard let index = notes.firstIndex(where: { $0.id == snapshot.id }) else {
                    return
                }
                notes[index] = updated
            }
        )
    }

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack {
            List {
                Section("Add synthetic note") {
                    TextField("New title", text: $newTitle)
                    Button("Add") { add() }
                        .disabled(newTitle.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines).isEmpty)
                }
                Section("Notes") {
                    ForEach(visibleNotes) { note in
                        NavigationLink {
                            NoteEditor(note: binding(for: note))
                        } label: {
                            Label(note.title.isEmpty ? "Untitled" : note.title,
                                  systemImage: note.finished ? "checkmark.circle" : "circle")
                        }
                    }
                    .onDelete { offsets in
                        let snapshot = visibleNotes
                        let ids = Set(offsets.compactMap { offset in
                            snapshot.indices.contains(offset) ? snapshot[offset].id : nil
                        })
                        notes.removeAll { ids.contains($0.id) }
                    }
                    .onMove { source, destination in
                        guard query.isEmpty else { return }
                        notes.move(fromOffsets: source, toOffset: destination)
                    }
                    if visibleNotes.isEmpty { Text("No matching notes") }
                }
                Section { Text(refreshMessage) }
            }
            .searchable(text: $query, prompt: "Find a title")
            .navigationTitle("Reading notes")
            .toolbar { EditButton().disabled(!query.isEmpty) }
            .refreshable { await refresh() }
        }
    }

    private func add() {
        let title = newTitle.trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines)
        guard !title.isEmpty else { return }
        notes.append(ReadingNote(title: title))
        newTitle = ""
    }

    private func refresh() async {
        let token = UUID()
        refreshToken = token
        do {
            try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300))
            try Task.checkCancellation()
            guard refreshToken == token else { return }
            refreshMessage = "Synthetic refresh completed; edits preserved"
        } catch {
            guard refreshToken == token, !Task.isCancelled else { return }
            refreshMessage = "Synthetic refresh failed"
        }
    }
}

@main
@MainActor
struct NotesLessonApp: App {
    var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { NotesScreen() } }
}

A Binding supplies read and write access to the original note. This custom binding looks up the ID each time it reads or writes. An old saved integer index could point to a different note after a move or delete. Here a missing record returns the saved snapshot for display and ignores writes. That is a limited safety choice, not full recovery. A production editor should also say that the record was removed and end or disable editing. The setter should never redirect an edit to another note just because positions changed.

The custom initializer uses a default UUID argument. Swift evaluates that argument for a new construction, so a newly added note receives a new stable identity even if its title repeats. Foundation supplies UUID and trimming. No imported company row type or helper is required by the sample.

sections.title: Check the draft when Add runs
sections.html:
A draft is input the user is still editing. newTitle keeps that raw String. The Button's disabled state checks a trimmed copy, removing leading and trailing spaces for eligibility. It leaves the typed source intact. The Add action checks the same rule again, creates a note, appends it, then clears the draft. A guard exits before mutation when nothing meaningful remains. This resembles an explicit Android event handler. The disabled appearance helps the user, while the action still enforces the rule at the point where it changes the source.

Editing uses a Form because the destination contains labeled inputs. That edit is live: every keystroke updates the note through its binding. Navigating back therefore preserves those changes. If the product needs Cancel to discard changes, the editor must own a temporary draft and perform an explicit commit instead; adding a Cancel label to this live-binding editor would not undo mutations. Lesson 080 demonstrates staged modal editing.

The sample permits an empty existing title and displays Untitled as its list label. That is a declared teaching policy, not an accidental inconsistency with Add. A real product could instead require validation before committing edits. Write that rule deliberately and test both creation and editing. Derived UI state helps communicate a rule; it does not decide the domain policy for you.

sections.title: Map visible positions before deleting
sections.html:
An offset is a position in one collection. onDelete reports offsets in visibleNotes, the collection passed to ForEach. If search hides A and shows B first, visible offset zero means B. Removing source index zero would wrongly delete A. The handler first snapshots the visible collection, reads IDs at the requested offsets, then removes those IDs from notes. A Set stores those chosen IDs for membership checks. Reading all selected IDs before mutation also avoids positions shifting during a multi-row delete.

Reordering means changing the source order, and search makes that rule ambiguous. Should visible matches move around hidden notes, or only within the filtered view? This example allows moves only when query is empty. It disables EditButton under search and also checks query in the move handler. The action guard still matters because not every call must come through that toolbar. Without a filter, visible and source order match, so the ordinary array move has a clear meaning.

Search results are derived state. Keep notes as the authoritative array rather than replacing it with the filtered array. Otherwise clearing search cannot recover hidden records, and editing can affect a copy. Stable IDs let you apply source mutations even as the displayed subset changes. This is the same correctness principle you use for Android list keys, while the SwiftUI callback shapes remain different.

sections.title: Await refresh and keep the edits
sections.html:
An asynchronous closure can wait for work without blocking a thread. refreshable awaits refresh directly so its progress display can follow that work's completion. Starting another unstructured Task and returning immediately would let this closure finish before the operation. The example waits briefly, checks cancellation, and changes a status message. It does not replace notes or contact a server. Cancellation is a request for cooperation. The synthetic delay can cooperate, but a later real service needs its own cancellation and merge rules.

A request token names this refresh attempt. A newer refresh replaces the current token, so an older attempt cannot later set the status over it. Both success and error check whether their token is current. The error path also rejects cancelled work rather than showing ordinary cancellation as a product failure. The short wait makes the learner demo visible. It does not decide a reliable test order. Use start signals and test-controlled completion gates for cancellation and old-result tests, as lessons 081 and 084 explain.

A real refresh that returns records needs a merge policy for unsaved edits, stable IDs, deletion, pagination and account changes. Do not reset notes to the original fixture merely to make a refresh look successful. A refresh indicator finishing proves only that the awaited closure ended; it does not prove the data is newer, persisted or correct. Report actual network and store boundaries separately when adding them.

sections.title: Try duplicates, hidden rows, and invalid input
sections.html:
A failure case is an input or sequence that can expose a wrong assumption. Add two notes with the same title, filter out earlier notes, then delete a visible match. Identify the removed record by its ID. Clear search and check what remains. Edit and reorder with no query, and verify that IDs stay fixed. Type spaces into Add and confirm no append occurs. These cases test the identity and action rules more directly than a screenshot of three ordinary rows. Record actual outcomes rather than treating the expected sequence as executed evidence.

The active demo's ContentView uses a List of destinations, providing a verified simple collection anchor. Its company FilterListView uses its own model and publisher contract; it is not the scratch store or proof of editable persistent-row identity. The beginner sample intentionally establishes IDs appropriate to mutable records before the more complex production material. Do not edit those client sources.

If a row jumps or loses editing state, inspect its identity first. If deletion removes a hidden record, inspect the visible-to-source mapping. If refresh erases typing, inspect the merge policy. If an editor updates a different row after reorder, inspect any captured index. A correct worked explanation can name each boundary without claiming that local State is a database.

exercise.brief: Add, edit, and delete in-memory notes. Use a filtered example to show that deletion removes the intended ID.
steps: Use the complete source and add two made-up notes with the same title.
Search so an earlier source row is hidden, then delete a visible match.
Clear search and identify the removed UUID, using a note of the IDs if needed.
Edit a title and reorder with an empty query. Verify each ID stays the same.
Run the synthetic refresh and check that your edits remain.
acceptance: Blank trimmed input is rejected at the action boundary.
Duplicate titles have distinct stable IDs.
Filtered deletion maps through visible IDs before mutating notes.
Reordering is explicitly disabled/guarded under search.
Refresh preserves edits and cancellation is not presented as a domain failure.
exercise.solution:
Use source order A, B, C, with search showing B, C. Deleting visible offset zero must remove B. Read B's UUID from that visible snapshot, then remove the matching source note. Clearing search should show A and C. Deleting source index zero instead would remove hidden A. This small sequence makes the mapping error checkable without relying on title uniqueness.

Editing a title uses the current ID lookup rather than a captured integer position, so moving the row cannot redirect a later write to another record. If a record disappears, this teaching binding ignores writes; a production editor should additionally present a removed-record state. The live-binding editor has no discard-on-back promise. Refresh changes only its synthetic status and awaits its own work, leaving the note array alone. A complete evidence note lists the fixture IDs, search term, removed ID and actual observed ordering. It marks simulator and cancellation checks as pending when they were not run. Disk-backed CRUD begins in lesson 083.

simple.story: Ada has three recipe cards with small permanent stickers: A, B, and C. She puts B and C on the table because those recipes mention soup. Lin asks her to remove the first card on the table. That means B, even though A is first in the drawer. Ada reads B's sticker and removes that card from the drawer. She does not use the table position as the drawer position. Changing B's title or moving its place would not change its sticker. The sticker identifies the card itself.
simple.meaning: Search produces a visible subset of notes. onDelete gives positions within that subset. Map those positions to stable IDs before changing the full source array. A title and an array position can both change while the record stays the same.

example.before: The source is [A: Demo arrays, B: Demo bindings, C: Demo bindings practice]. Searching bindings shows [B, C]. A, B, and C are labels for distinct UUIDs.
example.change: Delete visible offset 0 while the bindings search is active.
example.after: The source contains [A, C], and the visible matches contain [C]. Offset 0 meant B in the filtered collection, so the handler removes B's ID. Clearing search afterward will reveal that hidden A remained intact.

simple.boundary: SwiftUI's visible rows are recreated descriptions, not permanent physical cards. The example keeps records only in memory. Its refresh changes a synthetic status message; it does not fetch newer server records or save edits.
